title: Biotechnology
subtitle: Biological knowledge, genetic engineering and bioinformatics, and how Australia uses them
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: investigate the uses and applications of biotechnology (past, present and future), including: researching future directions of the use of biotechnology (ACSBL087)
Discuss the roles of biological knowledge, genetic engineering and bioinformatics techniques used in biotechnology
Use examples to explain how biotechnology is currently used in Australian research, agriculture, biodiversity conservation and health
Assess the role of data and modelling in developing and using biotechnology
inquiryQuestion: How do genetic techniques affect Earth's biodiversity?
lessonIntent: Students can define biotechnology broadly, explain the separate roles of biological knowledge, genetic engineering and bioinformatics using recombinant insulin, and give current Australian examples in research, agriculture, conservation and health.
examSkill: Identify the role that biological knowledge, genetic engineering and bioinformatics each play in a biotechnology, and support it with a specific Australian example.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, what biotechnology is, and the three tools it runs on. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: From cow pancreas to bacteria
scenes.body: For sixty years, people with diabetes injected insulin extracted from cattle and pig pancreases. In 1982, bacteria started making human insulin instead.
scenes.callout: What had to be known, built and computed before a bacterium could make a human hormone?
scenes.caption: Insulin moved from animal extraction in the 1920s to recombinant human insulin made by microbes in 1982.

voiceover.text: In the early nineteen twenties, researchers in Toronto showed that insulin extracted from a pancreas could keep people with type one diabetes alive. For the next sixty years, that insulin came from the pancreases of cattle and pigs, collected from abattoirs by the tonne. Then in nineteen eighty two, something remarkable was approved. Human insulin, made not by a human, but by bacteria carrying the human insulin gene, grown in huge steel fermentation tanks. Today most insulin is made by engineered microbes. So what had to happen first? Scientists had to understand insulin, they had to move a human gene into a microbe, and they had to handle a lot of sequence data. Those three things, biological knowledge, genetic engineering and bioinformatics, are what modern biotechnology runs on, and that's today's lesson.

scenes.heading: Using living systems for human purposes
scenes.body: Biotechnology is the use of living organisms, cells or biological processes to make products or solve problems.

bullets.text: Past: fermentation and selective breeding used organisms without understanding DNA.
Present: genetic engineering and sequencing act on DNA directly.
Future: gene editing, gene therapy and computer designed proteins.

scenes.secondary: The field is defined by using biological systems, not by how modern it looks. Brewing and gene editing both count.
scenes.callout: Defined by the biology used, not by how futuristic it looks.

diagram.beforeContent: Fermentation and selective breeding, using metabolism and inheritance without changing DNA.
diagram.afterContent: Genetic engineering, sequencing and bioinformatics, acting on DNA directly.

scenes.caption: Biotechnology uses living systems for human purposes, from fermentation to gene editing.

voiceover.text: So let's get the definition right, because a narrow one costs marks. Biotechnology is the use of living organisms, cells or biological processes to make products or to solve problems. That definition is deliberately broad. In the past, humans used fermentation for bread and beer, and selective breeding for crops and livestock, without knowing anything about DNA, and those still count as biotechnology. In the present, genetic engineering and DNA sequencing let us act on DNA directly. And the future is already arriving, with gene editing, gene therapy and proteins designed on computers. What ties it all together is the use of biological systems, not how modern the technology looks. Now let's zoom in on the modern toolkit, because it rests on three distinct roles.

scenes.heading: Three roles in modern biotechnology
scenes.body: Modern biotechnology combines biological knowledge, genetic engineering and bioinformatics. Each does a different job.

bullets.text: Biological knowledge: understanding what a gene or protein does, and why it matters.
Genetic engineering: physically changing DNA, like inserting a gene into a microbe.
Bioinformatics: using computing to store, search and analyse sequence data.

rows: Insulin's structure, and that type 1 diabetes lacks it
Insert the human insulin gene into bacteria or yeast
Store, search and check the gene and protein sequences

scenes.callout: Know it, change it, compute it.
scenes.caption: Biological knowledge explains, genetic engineering changes DNA, bioinformatics handles the data.

voiceover.text: Here's the framework the newer syllabus wants you to discuss. Modern biotechnology combines three roles, and each one does a different job. First, biological knowledge. You have to understand what a gene or protein does before you can use it. For insulin, that meant knowing its structure, and knowing that people with type one diabetes can't make it. Second, genetic engineering, which physically changes DNA. For insulin, the human insulin gene was inserted into bacteria, and later yeast, so the microbes would make the human protein. Third, bioinformatics, the use of computing to store, search and analyse biological data. Gene and protein sequences are stored in databases, and software checks that the product matches the human sequence exactly. So a simple way to remember it is, know it, change it, compute it.

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: Biotechnology: using living organisms, cells or biological processes to make products or solve problems.
Genetic engineering: directly altering an organism's DNA, often by adding a gene.
Recombinant DNA: DNA formed by joining genetic material from different sources.
Bioinformatics: using computing to store, compare and analyse biological data.
Model: a simplified representation, often computer based, used to make predictions.

scenes.callout: Genetic engineering is one tool within biotechnology, not the whole field.
scenes.caption: Biotechnology, genetic engineering, recombinant DNA, bioinformatics, model.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down the vocabulary. Biotechnology is using living organisms, cells or biological processes to make products or solve problems. Genetic engineering is directly altering an organism's DNA, very often by adding a gene from somewhere else. Recombinant DNA is the DNA that results, formed by joining genetic material from different sources, like a human gene joined into a bacterial plasmid. Bioinformatics is the use of computing to store, compare and analyse biological data. And a model is a simplified representation, often run on a computer, that we use to make predictions. Notice how they nest. Genetic engineering is one tool inside biotechnology, not the whole field.

scenes.heading: Data and modelling drive the field
scenes.body: Bioinformatics turns huge amounts of sequence data into predictions that guide what gets built.

bullets.text: Databases let researchers find a gene's sequence instead of working it out from scratch.
Computer models now predict a protein's 3D shape from its amino acid sequence.
Models also forecast outcomes, like how a GM crop's genes might spread.

scenes.secondary: Models are only as good as their data and assumptions, so predictions still need testing in the lab and the field.
scenes.callout: Models save time, but they still need testing.
scenes.caption: Databases and computer models guide biotechnology, but predictions must still be tested.

voiceover.text: Now, the role of data and modelling has exploded, so it's worth its own scene. Shared databases mean a researcher can look up a gene's sequence in seconds, instead of working it out from scratch. Computer models have gone even further. Programs can now predict the three dimensional shape of a protein from its amino acid sequence alone, which used to take years of lab work for each protein. That helps scientists design drugs and engineered proteins much faster. Models are also used to forecast outcomes, like how genes from a genetically modified crop might spread into nearby plants. But here's the balanced view. A model is only as good as its data and its assumptions, so its predictions still have to be tested in the lab and in the field. Models save time, they don't replace evidence.

scenes.heading: Biotechnology in Australia today
scenes.body: Australian examples show all three roles at work across research, agriculture, conservation and health.

bullets.text: Research and health: the HPV vaccine grew from University of Queensland research.
Agriculture: most Australian cotton carries Bt genes, cutting insecticide spraying.
Conservation: the koala genome, sequenced in 2018, guides disease and breeding decisions.

scenes.callout: Name the example, then name the role it relies on.
scenes.caption: HPV vaccine, Bt cotton and the koala genome show biotechnology across Australian sectors.

voiceover.text: Let's make it Australian, because the syllabus asks for current examples. In research and health, Ian Frazer and Jian Zhou at the University of Queensland developed the technology behind the HPV vaccine, which protects against the virus that causes most cervical cancers. The vaccine is made by engineered yeast that produce a harmless viral protein. In agriculture, most Australian cotton is genetically modified to carry genes from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis, so the plants make their own insecticide, and farmers spray far less. And in conservation, an Australian led team sequenced the koala genome in twenty eighteen. That data is used to understand koala diseases like chlamydia and a koala retrovirus, and to help manage genetic diversity in wild populations. So in an exam, name the example, then name the role it relies on.

scenes.heading: Identify the roles
scenes.question: For Bt cotton, identify how biological knowledge, genetic engineering and bioinformatics each contributed.
scenes.coachNote: Match each step to one role: understanding, changing DNA, or handling data.
steps: Biological knowledge: a soil bacterium makes Cry proteins that are toxic to certain caterpillars but not to people.
Genetic engineering: the Cry gene was inserted into the cotton genome, so the plant makes the protein itself.
Bioinformatics: gene sequences were stored and compared to design and check the inserted gene.
Data and modelling also guide resistance management, predicting how fast pests could adapt.
Answer: know the toxin, insert its gene, analyse the sequence data ✓
scenes.caption: Bt cotton: knowledge of the toxin, genetic engineering to insert it, bioinformatics to handle the sequences.

voiceover.text: Let's apply the three roles to one technology, Bt cotton. The method is to match each step to one role, understanding, changing DNA, or handling data. Biological knowledge came first. Scientists knew that a soil bacterium, Bacillus thuringiensis, makes Cry proteins that are toxic to certain caterpillars, but not to people or most other animals. Genetic engineering came next. The gene for a Cry protein was inserted into the cotton genome, so the plant makes the protein in its own leaves. And bioinformatics tied it together, because the gene sequences were stored and compared to design the inserted gene and check that it was correct. Data and modelling keep mattering after release too, because models predict how quickly pests could evolve resistance, which shapes how farmers plant the crop. So the answer in short is, know the toxin, insert its gene, analyse the sequence data.

scenes.heading: Two traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: defining biotechnology as only genetic engineering. Fermentation and selective breeding are biotechnology too, and genetic engineering is just one tool within it.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: treating bioinformatics as 'just computers'. It depends on biological knowledge to ask the right questions, and its predictions still have to be tested in living systems.
scenes.callout: Biotechnology is bigger than genetic engineering; bioinformatics is still biology.
scenes.caption: Genetic engineering is one tool in biotechnology; bioinformatics still relies on biology and testing.

voiceover.text: Two traps to avoid. Trap one, defining biotechnology as only genetic engineering. That's too narrow. Fermentation and selective breeding are biotechnology as well, and genetic engineering is just one tool inside the field. If your definition leaves out thousands of years of brewing and breeding, every later evaluation you write will be skewed. Trap two is newer, treating bioinformatics as if it were just computers. It isn't. Bioinformatics only works because biological knowledge tells it what questions to ask, like which gene to search for, or what a protein needs to do. And its predictions still have to be tested in real cells, plants and animals. So biotechnology is bigger than genetic engineering, and bioinformatics is still biology.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: Using recombinant human insulin, explain why it shows the shift from past to present biotechnology, and name the role each step relies on.
answerSteps: Past: insulin was extracted from cattle and pig pancreases, using animals without changing DNA.
Present: the human insulin gene is inserted into bacteria or yeast, which is genetic engineering.
That relied on biological knowledge of insulin's structure and role in diabetes.
Bioinformatics stores and checks the gene and protein sequences.
Answer: it moved from using animals to engineering microbes, drawing on all three roles ✓
scenes.caption: Insulin moved from animal extraction to engineered microbes, using knowledge, engineering and bioinformatics.

voiceover.text: Quick check. Using recombinant human insulin, explain why it shows the shift from past to present biotechnology, and name the role each step relies on. Pause and reason it through. Right. In the past, insulin was extracted from the pancreases of cattle and pigs, so it used animals as a source, without changing any DNA. In the present, the human insulin gene is inserted into bacteria or yeast, which then make human insulin, and that's genetic engineering. But that step depended on biological knowledge first, understanding insulin's structure and its role in diabetes. And bioinformatics is what stores and checks the gene and protein sequences, so the product matches human insulin exactly. So insulin moved from using animals to engineering microbes, and it draws on all three roles along the way.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Biotechnology is using living systems for human purposes, past, present and future.
Modern biotechnology combines biological knowledge, genetic engineering and bioinformatics.
Data and modelling speed up design, but predictions still need testing.
Australian examples: HPV vaccine, Bt cotton and the koala genome.
Genetic engineering is one tool within biotechnology, not the whole field.
scenes.finalPrompt: For any biotechnology, ask: what knowledge did it need, what DNA did it change, and what data did it use?
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: the definition, three roles, data and modelling, Australian examples, the big trap.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five takeaways. First, biotechnology is the use of living systems for human purposes, and it covers the past, the present and the future. Second, modern biotechnology combines three roles, biological knowledge, genetic engineering and bioinformatics. Third, data and modelling speed up design enormously, but their predictions still need testing. Fourth, you've got three Australian examples ready to use, the HPV vaccine, Bt cotton and the koala genome. And fifth, genetic engineering is one tool within biotechnology, not the whole field. So for any biotechnology, ask what knowledge it needed, what DNA it changed, and what data it used.
